div.head: Ine 11
div.ab: LV. Gif hwa his agenne geleod bebycgge, ðeowne oððe frigne, ðeah he scyldig sie, ofer sæ, forgielde hine his were.
LV. . . . geleod bebycge, þeow . . ., þeah he scildig sie, ofer . ., . . lde hine his were.
LV. Gif hwa his agenne leod gebycge, ðeowne oððe frigne, þeah he scyldig sy, ofer sǽ gesylle, forgilde hine be his were.
Be landbygene. Gyf hwa his ágene leodan bebicge, ðeowne oððe frige, þeah he scyldig sy, ofer sǽ, forgylde hine be his wére (⁊ wið Godd deoplice bete).
Si quis compatriotam suum emat seruum uel liberum, licet reus sit, ultra mare, soluat eum wera sua.
[Be landbygene.] Gif hwa his agenne geleod bebycgge, ðeowne oððe frigne, ðeah he scyldig sie, ofer sæ, forgielde hine his were [⁊ wið Godd deoplice bete]
{LV} Gif hwa his agenne geleod bebycgge, ðeowne oððe frigne, ðeah he scyldig sie, ofer sæ, forgielde hine his were.
Wenn jemand seinen eigenen Landsmann über See verkauft, einen Sklaven oder Freien, selbst wenn derselbe schuldig ist, löse er sich mit seinem Wergeld (und büsse tief gegenüber Gott).
If someone sells his own countryman over the sea, a slave or a free man, even if the latter is guilty, let him redeem himself with his wergeld (and make deep amends towards God).
If anyone sells one of his own countrymen, bond or free, over the sea, even though he be guilty, he shall pay for him with his wergeld and make full atonement with God [for his crime].
If anyone sells his own countryman, bond or free, even if he is guilty, across the sea, he is to pay for him with his [own] wergild.
If someone sells over the sea his own countryman, slave or free, even though he is guilty [of an offense], let him compensate by payment of his [own] wer.

Nicht Verkaufter oder seine Sippe hat einen Anspruch, da jener ja als Verbrecher friedlos geworden ist, sondern der König, wie bei Friesen; s. Gl Heidentum 3. Q (der Neuere verführt) missversteht das reflexive hine als eum ‘Verkauften’. Der Fall ist aber ein anderer als rechtswidrige Verknechtung (s. d. Gl 3), wofür dieses Wergeld dem Verkauften bei anderen Germanen zufällt; Brunner II 615. Der hier miterwähnte Unfreie hat ja kein Wergeld. Des Verbrechers Wergeld (s. d. Gl 26. 30) also ist gemeint

It is not the man sold or his kindred that has a claim, since he has after all become an outlaw as a criminal, but the king, as among the Frisians; see Gl Heidentum 3. Q (who leads modern scholars astray) misunderstands the reflexive hine as eum, ‘the man sold’. But the case is a different one from unlawful enslavement (see that word in Gl 3), for which among other Germanic peoples this wergild goes to the man sold; Brunner II 615. The unfree man also mentioned here has, after all, no wergild. It is therefore the criminal’s wergild (see that word in Gl 26. 30) that is meant
Zusatz nur B cor., daraus Ld. ‘Einfluss der Kirche’ auf Ine oder Ælfred also folgt nicht hieraus
Addition only in B cor., whence Ld. No ‘influence of the Church’ on Ine or Ælfred, then, follows from this

i.e. only a West Saxon.
i.e. a freeman who has been reduced to slavery.

Liebermann translates—‘löse er sich mit seinem Wergeld.’ Grammatically his could refer to ‘the countryman bond or free,’ but this interpretation would be open to the objection that the slave has no wergeld. At this time an export trade in slaves was carried on in London by Frisian merchants; see the case of Imma mentioned by Bede (Hist. Eccl. iv. 22). For earlier evidence of a similar practice see the account of Gregory and the English slaves given by Bede (op. cit. ii. 1).
